claim: Approximately 64% of mouse CR studies since 2003 used males only.
source: We found that male-only studies predominated for mice, accounting for ~64% of all mouse CR studies since 2003 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, which show the cumulative publications and percentages of mouse CR studies by sex composition.

claim: Fewer than 20% of mouse CR studies used females only.
source: Fewer than 20% of studies used females only, while around 7.3% combined males and females, suggesting an assumption that sex would not influence experimental outcomes.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by the systematic review data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Around 7.3% of mouse CR studies combined males and females.
source: Fewer than 20% of studies used females only, while around 7.3% combined males and females, suggesting an assumption that sex would not influence experimental outcomes.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and is supported by the systematic review data.

claim: Approximately 60% of human CR studies combined males and females.
source: In contrast,~60% of human studies combined males and females, while ~23% used only females and ~12% only males (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Approximately 23% of human CR studies used only females.
source: In contrast,~60% of human studies combined males and females, while ~23% used only females and ~12% only males (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Approximately 12% of human CR studies used only males.
source: In contrast,~60% of human studies combined males and females, while ~23% used only females and ~12% only males (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: By the end of 2021, studies that included both sexes and analysed data with sex as a variable were in a minority for both mice (~3.4%) and humans (~4.5%).
source: Strikingly, by the end of 2021, studies that included both sexes and analysed data with sex as a variable were in a minority for both mice (~3.4%) and humans (~4.5%) (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1A and 1C.

claim: The proportion of studies using each sex or combination of sexes has remained relatively constant since 2003.
source: Moreover, the proportion of studies using each sex or combination of sexes has remained relatively constant since 2003 (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the trend data shown in Figure 1A and 1C.

claim: Efforts to increase the consideration of sex in experimental design have had little impact on the field of CR research.
source: Thus, efforts to increase the consideration of sex in experimental design, as promoted by the European Commission (Lee, 2018), Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) and National Institutes of Health (NIH) (Johnson et al., 2014), appear to have had little impact on the field of CR research.
evidence: The claim is based on the observation that the proportion of studies considering sex has remained constant despite policy initiatives, as shown in Figure 1.

claim: Results in approximately 74% of mouse studies that considered sex indicated a sex difference in the CR response.
source: We found that results in ~74% of mouse studies (Figure 1B) and ~62% of human studies (Figure 1D) indicated a sex difference in the CR response.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Results in approximately 62% of human studies that considered sex indicated a sex difference in the CR response.
source: We found that results in ~74% of mouse studies (Figure 1B) and ~62% of human studies (Figure 1D) indicated a sex difference in the CR response.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: CR decreased body mass in both male and female mice, but this effect was greater in males.
source: As expected, CR decreased body mass in both males and females (Figure 2A) but this effect was greater in males, with ANOVA confirming a significant sex-diet interaction.
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 2A showing body mass changes over time.

claim: CR decreased fat mass in males but females maintained fat mass.
source: CR decreased fat and lean mass in males, whereas females maintained fat mass and lost only lean mass (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by body composition data shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: CR decreased lean mass in both males and females.
source: CR decreased fat and lean mass in males, whereas females maintained fat mass and lost only lean mass (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by body composition data shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: A significant sex-diet interaction was apparent for absolute fat mass.
source: A significant sex-diet interaction was apparent for absolute fat mass (Figure 2C) and for fat mass relative to baseline (Figure 2D)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: CR decreased the absolute mass of gonadal, inguinal, mesenteric, and perirenal WAT depots in males but not females.
source: We found that in males but not females CR decreased the absolute mass of gonadal (gWAT), inguinal (iWAT), mesenteric (mWAT), and perirenal (pWAT) WAT depots, as well as brown adipose tissue (BAT; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by tissue mass data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CR decreased brown adipose tissue mass in males but not females.
source: We found that in males but not females CR decreased the absolute mass of gonadal (gWAT), inguinal (iWAT), mesenteric (mWAT), and perirenal (pWAT) WAT depots, as well as brown adipose tissue (BAT; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by tissue mass data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The sex-diet interaction persisted for gWAT, iWAT, mWAT and pWAT when analyzed as % body mass.
source: This showed that the significant sex-diet interaction persisted for gWAT, iWAT, mWAT and pWAT.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of adipose depot masses as percentage of body mass, as described in the text and shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: CR significantly decreased average adipocyte area in males but not in females for gWAT.
source: CR significantly decreased average adipocyte area in males but not in females, both for gWAT (Figure 2H–I) and for mWAT (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by histomorphometric analysis data shown in Figure 2H-I.

claim: CR significantly decreased average adipocyte area in males but not in females for mWAT.
source: CR significantly decreased average adipocyte area in males but not in females, both for gWAT (Figure 2H–I) and for mWAT (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by histomorphometric analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: CR increased plasma NEFA concentrations in males but not in females.
source: Consistent with this, CR increased plasma NEFA concentrations in males but not in females (Figure 2J).
evidence: The claim is supported by plasma NEFA measurement data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: CR stimulated HSL phosphorylation in males but not in females.
source: CR stimulated HSL phosphorylation in males but not in females (Figure 2K–L, Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis data shown in Figure 2K-L and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Females resist lipolysis during CR.
source: Together, these observations show that females resist lipolysis during CR.
evidence: The claim is based on multiple lines of evidence including adipocyte size, plasma NEFA, and HSL phosphorylation data.

claim: CR decreased total energy expenditure in both sexes, with greater decreases occurring during week 3 compared to week 1.
source: This revealed that CR decreased total energy expenditure in both sexes, with greater decreases occurring during week 3 compared to week 1, and during nighttime compared to daytime (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: During week 1, CR females had lower daytime, nighttime, and total energy expenditure than CR males.
source: Notably, during week 1, CR females had lower daytime, nighttime, and total energy expenditure than CR males (Figure 3A–B), likely explaining females' resistance to weight loss and fat loss during the first week of CR (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by indirect calorimetry data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: CR decreased energy expenditure more in females than in males during week 1.
source: Together, these data show that CR decreases energy expenditure more in females than in males, despite increasing physical activity, and that factors beyond decreased lean mass contribute to this CR effect.
evidence: The claim is based on indirect calorimetry data and analysis of energy expenditure relative to lean mass.

claim: CR increased total and daytime physical activity in both sexes.
source: In contrast to these decreases in energy expenditure, CR increased total and daytime physical activity in both sexes, with CR females having higher activity than CR males during week 1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by activity monitoring data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Postprandial RER was greater in females than in males during CR, particularly during week 1.
source: Notably, this postprandial RER was greater in females than in males, particularly during week 1 (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RER data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: CR increased absolute FA oxidation in both sexes during week 1, but not during week 3.
source: As shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C, CR increased absolute FA oxidation in both sexes during week 1, but not during week 3.
evidence: The claim is supported by FA oxidation data calculated from energy expenditure and RER, shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: CR increased FA oxidation more in males than females.
source: Across both timepoints there was a significant sex-diet interaction, with CR increasing FA oxidation more in males than females (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by FA oxidation data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Females have greater postprandial FA synthesis and lower absolute FA oxidation than males during CR.
source: Together, these data show that females have greater postprandial FA synthesis and lower absolute FA oxidation than males, particularly during the first week of CR.
evidence: The claim is based on RER and FA oxidation data from indirect calorimetry.

claim: CR decreased blood glucose to a greater extent in males than in females.
source: We found that CR decreased blood glucose to a greater extent in males than in females (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by blood glucose measurement data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CR improved glucose tolerance in both sexes, but this effect was greater in males.
source: Consistent with this, oral glucose tolerance tests (OGTT) revealed that CR improved glucose tolerance in both sexes, but this effect was greater in males (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by OGTT data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Differences in fasting glucose are the main driver of CR-induced improvements in glucose tolerance and the sex differences therein.
source: These diet and sex effects were reflected by the OGTT total area under the curve (tAUC), calculated against 0 mM blood glucose; however, they were not apparent for the incremental AUC (iAUC), calculated against fasting blood glucose for each mouse (Figure 4C). This suggests that differences in fasting glucose are the main driver of CR-induced improvements in glucose tolerance and the sex differences therein.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of OGTT tAUC and iAUC data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CR decreased plasma insulin in males but not in females.
source: CR decreased plasma insulin in males but not in females, largely because AL females were already relatively hypoinsulinaemic (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by insulin ELISA data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CR significantly decreased HOMA-IR across both sexes, but within each sex the CR effect was significant for males only.
source: Across both sexes CR significantly decreased HOMA-IR and increased the Matsuda Index; however, within each sex the CR effect was significant for males only, indicating that females resist CR-induced improvements in insulin sensitivity (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by HOMA-IR calculation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CR significantly increased the Matsuda Index across both sexes, but within each sex the CR effect was significant for males only.
source: Across both sexes CR significantly decreased HOMA-IR and increased the Matsuda Index; however, within each sex the CR effect was significant for males only, indicating that females resist CR-induced improvements in insulin sensitivity (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Matsuda Index calculation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Females resist CR-induced improvements in insulin sensitivity.
source: Across both sexes CR significantly decreased HOMA-IR and increased the Matsuda Index; however, within each sex the CR effect was significant for males only, indicating that females resist CR-induced improvements in insulin sensitivity (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is based on HOMA-IR and Matsuda Index data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The sex-dependent effect of CR on body mass, fat mass, lean mass and WAT mass was conserved when CR diet was provided in the evening instead of the morning.
source: Consistently, we found that the sex-dependent effect of CR on body mass, fat mass, lean mass and WAT mass was conserved (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from evening-fed mice shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A-H.

claim: The diet and sex effects on glucose homeostasis persisted when CR diet was provided in the evening.
source: Similarly, an OGTT revealed that the diet and sex effects on glucose homeostasis persisted (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by OGTT data from evening-fed mice shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: CR improves glucose tolerance without any marked increases in peripheral glucose uptake.
source: Our PET/CT data show that CR improves glucose tolerance without any marked increases in peripheral glucose uptake (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by PET/CT imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: CR does not affect glucose uptake in the BMAT-rich distal tibia.
source: This includes the BMAT-rich distal tibia, suggesting that, although BMAT has high basal glucose uptake (Suchacki et al., 2020), increased BMAT glucose uptake is not required for improved glucose tolerance during CR.
evidence: The claim is based on PET/CT data and is supported by citation to previous work on BMAT glucose uptake.

claim: CR increases glucose uptake in WAT and the kidneys.
source: However, across both sexes, CR tended to increase glucose uptake in iWAT and gWAT and this effect was significant when assessed across all WAT depots (Figure 5C). CR also significantly increased glucose uptake in the kidneys (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by gamma counting data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Sex does not significantly alter the effect of CR on glucose uptake in any of the tissues assessed.
source: Notably, however, sex did not significantly alter the effect of CR in any of the tissues assessed.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of PET/CT and gamma counting data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The sexually dimorphic effects of CR on glucose homeostasis are not a result of CR increasing glucose disposal to a greater extent in males than in females.
source: Thus, the sexually dimorphic effects of CR on glucose homeostasis are not a result of CR increasing glucose disposal to a greater extent in males than in females.
evidence: The claim is based on the lack of sex differences in CR-induced changes in glucose uptake across tissues.

claim: Gross hepatic triglyceride content was not affected by diet or sex.
source: Because gross hepatic triglyceride content was not affected by diet or sex (Figure 6A), we undertook a more-detailed molecular investigation of lipid species that may underpin altered hepatic glucose regulation, focussing on sphingolipids (Petersen and Shulman, 2017; Chaurasia et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by hepatic triglyceride measurement data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Total ceramide content was significantly lower in females than in males but was not influenced by CR.
source: Targeted lipidomics revealed that total ceramide content was significantly lower in females than in males but was not influenced by CR (Figure 6B)
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS lipidomics data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 22:0 and 22:1 ceramides were lower in females than in males and were decreased by CR, with this diet effect being stronger in males.
source: Thus, 22:0 and 22:1 ceramides were lower in females than in males and were decreased by CR, with this diet effect being stronger in males (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS lipidomics data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 23:0 ceramides were greater in AL females than in AL males and were increased by CR in males only.
source: Conversely, 23:0 ceramides were greater in AL females than in AL males and were increased by CR in males only (Figure 6B)
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS lipidomics data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Total DHCs were lower in females than in males.
source: As for total ceramides, total DHCs were lower in females than in males; however, unlike for total ceramides, CR increased total DHCs in males only (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS lipidomics data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: CR increased total DHCs in males only.
source: As for total ceramides, total DHCs were lower in females than in males; however, unlike for total ceramides, CR increased total DHCs in males only (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS lipidomics data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The overall ceramide:DHC ratio was decreased by CR in males but not in females.
source: The overall ceramide:DHC ratio was decreased by CR in males but not in females (Figure 6C)
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS lipidomics data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Principal component analysis of ceramide data identified AL males as the most distinct group, with CR males being more similar to females on either diet.
source: Consistent with this, principal component analysis of these ceramide data identified AL males as the most distinct group, with CR males being more similar to females on either diet (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: CR suppresses ceramide synthesis to a greater extent in males than in females.
source: Together, these data indicate that CR suppresses ceramide synthesis to a greater extent in males than in females, highlighting a potential mechanism for CR's sexually dimorphic effects on glucose homeostasis.
evidence: The claim is based on the ceramide and dihydroceramide data and represents an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Principal component analysis of RNA-seq data identified AL males as the most transcriptionally distinct group, while CR males were more similar to AL or CR females.
source: Principal component analysis of this RNA-seq data identified AL males as the most transcriptionally distinct group, while CR males were more similar to AL or CR females (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Hundreds of genes were differentially expressed between males and females within each diet group.
source: Volcano plots further revealed the substantial effects of sex and diet on hepatic gene expression (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B): hundreds of genes were differentially expressed between males and females within each diet group (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) and between AL and CR mice, both within and across the two sexes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by volcano plot analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Gluconeogenesis-related genes were significantly increased with CR in each sex, but were more highly expressed in males than in females during CR.
source: Gluconeogenesis-related genes were significantly increased with CR in each sex, but, against our expectations, they were more highly expressed in males than in females during CR (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Genes related to oxidative phosphorylation and the TCA cycle increased with CR in males but not in females.
source: The greatest difference between CR males and CR females was for genes related to oxidative phosphorylation and the TCA cycle, which increased with CR in males but not in females (Figure 7C)
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Glycolysis-related genes were increased by CR, more so in males.
source: Glycolysis-related genes were also increased by CR, more so in males, whereas transcripts relevant to FA β-oxidation and FA biosynthesis were increased by CR in both sexes (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Transcripts relevant to FA β-oxidation and FA biosynthesis were increased by CR in both sexes.
source: Glycolysis-related genes were also increased by CR, more so in males, whereas transcripts relevant to FA β-oxidation and FA biosynthesis were increased by CR in both sexes (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Plasma ketones were significantly higher in females than males, particularly during CR.
source: Consistent with our model, plasma ketones were significantly higher in females than males, particularly during CR (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by blood ketone measurement data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: During CR, both sexes increase FA β-oxidation to generate acetyl-CoA and this is supported by increased FA biosynthesis.
source: These gene expression profiles support the following model (Figure 7D): during CR, both sexes increase FA β-oxidation to generate acetyl-CoA and this is supported by increased FA biosynthesis.
evidence: The claim is based on interpretation of RNA-seq data and is presented as a model in Figure 7D.

claim: Males, more than females, increase glycolysis for acetyl-CoA production during CR.
source: Males, more than females, also increase glycolysis for acetyl-CoA production; however, males utilise the acetyl-CoA to support increased TCA cycle activity and oxidative phosphorylation, pathways that are not increased by CR in females.
evidence: The claim is based on interpretation of RNA-seq data and is presented as part of the model.

claim: Males utilise hepatic acetyl-CoA to support the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation during CR.
source: Based on these data, our model is that CR males utilise hepatic acetyl-CoA to support the TCA cycle and ATP generation via oxidative phosphorylation
evidence: The claim is based on interpretation of RNA-seq and ketone data and is presented as part of the model.

claim: In CR females, hepatic acetyl-CoA accumulates, thereby stimulating pyruvate carboxylase and promoting gluconeogenesis.
source: in contrast, in CR females the hepatic acetyl-CoA accumulates, thereby stimulating pyruvate carboxylase and promoting gluconeogenesis (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is based on interpretation of RNA-seq and ketone data and is presented as part of the model.

claim: Females are better at resisting hypoglycaemia during CR.
source: Consequently, females are better at resisting hypoglycaemia during CR.
evidence: The claim is based on the proposed model of hepatic metabolism and is supported by blood glucose data.

claim: CR significantly stimulates oestrogen response pathways.
source: Another intriguing finding from our RNA-seq data is that CR significantly stimulates oestrogen response pathways (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Unlike in young mice, CR decreased body mass and fat mass to a similar extent in aged males and females.
source: Unlike in young mice, CR decreased body mass and fat mass to a similar extent in aged males and females, while the decreases in lean mass were greater in aged females (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by body composition data from aged mice shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: The decreases in lean mass during CR were greater in aged females than aged males.
source: Unlike in young mice, CR decreased body mass and fat mass to a similar extent in aged males and females, while the decreases in lean mass were greater in aged females (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by body composition data from aged mice shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: CR's effects on the masses of individual WAT depots did not differ between aged males and females.
source: Consistent with this, CR's effects on the masses of individual WAT depots did not differ between the sexes (Figure 8D, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by tissue mass data from aged mice shown in Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Unlike in young mice, aged males and females show a similar effect of CR on overall adiposity.
source: Thus, unlike in young mice, aged males and females show a similar effect of CR on overall adiposity and this is driven predominantly by loss of WAT.
evidence: The claim is based on body composition and tissue mass data from aged mice.

claim: In aged mice, the ability of CR to decrease fasting blood glucose was not significantly influenced by sex.
source: As shown in Figure 9A, in aged mice the ability of CR to decrease fasting blood glucose was not significantly influenced by sex.
evidence: The claim is supported by blood glucose data from aged mice shown in Figure 9A.

claim: CR improved glucose tolerance to a similar extent in aged males and females.
source: CR improved glucose tolerance to a similar extent in aged males and females, with tAUC but not iAUC being significantly decreased with CR (Figure 9B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by OGTT data from aged mice shown in Figure 9B-C.

claim: In aged mice, CR improves glucose tolerance primarily by decreasing fasting glucose.
source: The latter indicates that, as for young mice, CR improves glucose tolerance in aged mice primarily by decreasing fasting glucose.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of OGTT tAUC and iAUC data from aged mice.

claim: Sex differences in the metabolic effects of CR are highly age dependent.
source: However, overall, these studies demonstrate that sex differences in the metabolic effects of CR are highly age dependent, with CR being equally effective in aged males and females whereas young females resist these aspects of the CR response.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of data from young and aged mice.

claim: In humans, body mass and fat-free mass decreased more in males than in females during CR.
source: As in young mice, body mass and fat-free (lean) mass decreased more so in males than in females, with males also showing a trend for greater fold-decreases in total fat mass (Figure 10A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by body composition data from human subjects shown in Figure 10A-F.

claim: When adjusted for age, fold-change in body mass differed significantly between males and females during CR in humans.
source: When adjusted for age (Figure 10G), fold-change in body mass differed significantly between males and females (P, Intercept = 0.025).
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 10G.

claim: Overall weight loss is greater in males than females during CR in humans, independent of age.
source: This demonstrates that overall weight loss is greater in males than females, independent of age.
evidence: The claim is based on linear regression analysis of human body mass data.

claim: The decreases in fat mass during CR in humans were sex- and age-dependent.
source: In contrast, the decreases in fat mass and fat-free mass were sex- and age-dependent. Thus, fat loss in younger individuals was greater in males than females but, with age, fat loss increased in females but diminished in males (Figure 10H) (P, Slope = 0.007).
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 10H.

claim: Fat loss in younger individuals was greater in males than females, but with age, fat loss increased in females but diminished in males.
source: Thus, fat loss in younger individuals was greater in males than females but, with age, fat loss increased in females but diminished in males (Figure 10H) (P, Slope = 0.007).
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 10H.

claim: The loss of fat-free mass in younger individuals was greater in females than in males and this relationship reversed in older individuals.
source: Conversely, the loss of fat-free mass in younger individuals was greater in females than in males and this relationship reversed in older individuals (Figure 10I).
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 10I.

claim: The relationship between age and loss of fat-free mass differed significantly between the sexes during CR in humans.
source: As for fat mass, the relationship between age and loss of fat-free mass differed significantly between the sexes (P, Slope = 0.0004).
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 10I.

claim: The sex differences in loss of fat mass or fat-free mass were unrelated to fat mass or BMI at baseline in humans.
source: In contrast, the sex differences in loss of fat mass or fat-free mass were unrelated to fat mass or BMI at baseline (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only in the younger age group (<45 years) did males show greater fat loss than females during CR in humans.
source: Total weight loss was greater in males than females regardless of age (Figure 10J), but only in the younger age group did males show greater fat loss than females (Figure 10K).
evidence: The claim is supported by age-stratified analysis shown in Figure 10K.

claim: Males' greater loss of fat-free mass occurred only in the older age group (>45 years) during CR in humans.
source: Conversely, males' greater loss of fat-free mass occurred only in the older age group (Figure 10L).
evidence: The claim is supported by age-stratified analysis shown in Figure 10L.

claim: The ability of CR to decrease body mass, fat mass and lean mass is sex- and age-dependent in both mice and humans.
source: Thus, our data demonstrate that the ability of CR to decrease body mass, fat mass and lean mass is sex- and age-dependent in both mice and humans.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of data from mice and humans across different ages.

claim: CR extends lifespan and reduces the risk of age-related diseases in numerous species, ranging from yeast to primates.
source: CR extends lifespan and reduces the risk of age-related diseases in numerous species, ranging from yeast to primates (Lin et al., 2002; Weindruch et al., 1986; Mattison et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Trials of CR in humans show numerous health benefits, including the prevention of cardiovascular disease, hypertension, obesity, type 2 diabetes, chronic inflammation, and risk of certain cancers.
source: however, trials of CR in humans show numerous health benefits, including the prevention of cardiovascular disease, hypertension, obesity, type 2 diabetes, chronic inflammation, and risk of certain cancers (Most et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: The ability of CR to promote healthy ageing is now also recognised in humans.
source: Thus, the ability of CR to promote healthy ageing is now also recognised in humans.
evidence: The claim is based on the cited evidence of health benefits in humans.

claim: Ageing is characterised by hepatic insulin resistance, hyperinsulinaemia, and excessive accumulation of white adipose tissue, particularly visceral WAT.
source: Ageing is characterised by hepatic insulin resistance, hyperinsulinaemia, and excessive accumulation of white adipose tissue (WAT), particularly visceral WAT (Barzilai et al., 1998; López-Otín et al., 2016; Mancuso and Bouchard, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Adipose dysfunction during ageing results in ectopic lipid accumulation in the liver and other tissues, contributing to insulin resistance and metabolic dysregulation.
source: The latter is coupled with adipose dysfunction, whereby WAT becomes unable to meet the demands for safe lipid storage. This results in ectopic lipid accumulation in the liver and other tissues, contributing to insulin resistance and metabolic dysregulation (Barzilai et al., 1998; Mancuso and Bouchard, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: CR counteracts the effects of ageing by decreasing WAT mass, increasing fatty acid oxidation, preventing ectopic lipid deposition and enhancing insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance.
source: CR counteracts these effects, decreasing WAT mass, increasing fatty acid (FA) oxidation, preventing ectopic lipid deposition and enhancing insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance (Speakman and Mitchell, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Removal of visceral WAT, independent of CR, is sufficient to prevent insulin resistance, improve glucose tolerance and increase lifespan in rodents.
source: Notably, studies in rodents show that removal of visceral WAT, independent of CR, is sufficient to prevent insulin resistance, improve glucose tolerance and increase lifespan (Gabriely et al., 2002; Muzumdar et al., 2008; Tran et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Visceral WAT loss in humans is strongly associated with CR's metabolic benefits.
source: Visceral WAT loss in humans is also strongly associated with CR's metabolic benefits (Larson-Meyer et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published research.
